Investing.com -- Taiwan is emerging as the biggest domestic beneficiary of Asia's artificial intelligence export boom, followed by South Korea, as stronger technology demand boosts economic activity, government revenues and investment, according to Bank of America.
The bank said AI-related exports have become a major growth driver for Taiwan, South Korea and China, although the economic benefits are spreading unevenly across the three markets.
Year-to-date exports have increased 57% year over year in South Korea, 44% in Taiwan and 21% in China, according to BofA's analysis.
Despite South Korea recording the strongest export growth, Taiwan is expected to experience the largest domestic spillover effects.
BofA attributed the differences to the relative size of each economy's technology sector, production capacity constraints and broader economic conditions.
Taiwan's substantial exposure to technology manufacturing means stronger external demand can translate into wider domestic economic gains.
South Korea also stands to benefit significantly, with the export expansion supporting domestic activity and government finances.
China is benefiting from stronger technology exports, but weaker domestic demand and economic headwinds are limiting the broader impact.
The differences are also shaping fiscal policy across the region.
BofA said rising exports have increased government tax revenues in all three economies, creating opportunities for additional public spending.
In Taiwan and South Korea, higher fiscal receipts are helping finance transfers and investment, providing another channel through which export growth supports domestic demand.
China has not experienced a comparable spending boost, partly reflecting financial constraints facing local governments.
The uneven economic effects are expected to produce different monetary policy responses.
In Taiwan and South Korea, stronger domestic demand and positive output gaps are adding to inflationary pressures, supporting the case for further interest rate increases.
China faces a different outlook, with softer domestic demand pointing toward additional monetary easing.
BofA's assessment suggests Taiwan and South Korea are positioned to capture stronger economy-wide benefits from the AI boom, with China's gains remaining more concentrated amid domestic challenges.

Binance began restoring customer withdrawals Sunday after hackers drained over $6 billion in the biggest cyber theft ever recorded, as the crypto industry awaits answers on the breach blamed on North Korea and steps to strengthen the exchange’s defenses.
The world’s largest digital-asset platform reopened Bitcoin withdrawals after 2 p.m. Singapore time, more than two days after halting them following the breach. By evening in Asia, the exchange had seen some $3.5 billion in net outflows, according to DefiLlama data. Co-Chief Executive Officer Yi He said on X some transfers are between Binance wallets.
The first phase of withdrawals covers 15 tokens, including Ether and the two biggest stablecoins, Tether’s USDT and Circle Internet Group Inc.’s USDC, Binance said on X. Withdrawals on 15 blockchain networks including Ethereum, BNB Smart Chain, XRP and Base resumed by around 8:30 p.m. in Singapore, according to the company.
Read more: Binance’s $6.3 Billion Hack: How Crypto Insurance Works
Binance dwarfs its industry rivals, with roughly $132 billion in assets, compared with about $29 billion at the second-largest exchange OKX. “We are taking a phased approach by prioritizing tokens based on the past week data of user demand, so that each network and asset pair can be restored carefully, with stability and security checks completed before access is reopened,” Binance said.
Quantitative trading firm SQS Trading has about a quarter of its trading capital on Binance, and is cutting that by roughly a third, according to founder Eli Williams, who added that it won’t flatten positions or reduce usage of the exchange as a venue for hedging. “It’s hard to forecast what the net impact will be at this point but we will be monitoring capital outflows and volume impact relative to other major venues,” Williams said.
Others are holding off any changes. Justin d’Anethan, head of research at Arctic Digital, a private markets advisory firm, said he’s not fazed by the hack. “When something seems fishy, it’s good to act fast; but when something catastrophic happens, it’s better to hold off doing anything,” he said. “I haven’t and wouldn’t move away from Binance.”
A spokesperson for Binance said the withdrawal volumes “spiked at the beginning,” but are now stabilizing to what the company considers normal activity, and a small percentage of its overall assets under management.
The restart tests Binance’s promise to make customers whole following a theft four times the size of the previous record crypto hack at Bybit in 2025. The US Federal Bureau of Investigation said on Saturday the Binance attack was carried out by TraderTraitor, an elite North Korean hacking unit it also held responsible for the roughly $1.5 billion Bybit theft.
The market fallout appears relatively contained, with most major cryptocurrencies seeing a change of less than 1% Sunday. Bitcoin, which accounts for about 60% of the sector’s market value, was trading around $78,000, about 5% below its Thursday high before the attack.
“On some level, this shows how much the industry has matured,” said Haseeb Qureshi, managing partner at venture fund Dragonfly. “We saw extraordinarily quick responses.”
Binance said it has so far replaced about 95% of the stolen cryptocurrency using its corporate treasury, emergency funds and insurance funds. The funds drained in the attack were a mix of the largest cryptocurrencies across 10 blockchains, including Bitcoin and Ethereum.

It’s been a long and winding journey for Zouhair Talbi to realize his American dream, but winning the Houston Marathon in 2:05.45 on January 11 as a U.S. citizen was only part of that dream coming true.
The 31-year-old Moroccan-born runner ran the third-fastest time ever by a U.S. runner on a record-eligible course—behind only American record holder Conner Mantz (2:04:43 in Chicago last fall) and Khalid Khannouchi (2:05:38 in London in 2002)—taking nearly a minute off his personal best set two years earlier in Houston when he ran under his Moroccan citizenship in his lead-up to the Paris Olympics.
But not long after he celebrated at the finish line with an American flag draped over his shoulders, Zouhair relished another milestone moment as his wife, Elizabeth Talbi, 23, also had a breakthrough result in the marathon, placing 10th among women in 2:35:26—a 15-minute personal best from her debut effort in 2024—just 10 months after giving birth to their son, Amir.
Moreover, they each surpassed the qualifying standards for the 2028 U.S. Olympic Trials Marathon, which means they’ll both be on the starting line of the races that will determine who will make the U.S. team for the Los Angeles Olympics. The race will either be in Phoenix or St. Louis, and it is tentatively scheduled for the weekend of March 25-26, 2028. In other words, after August 2027, when Zouhair becomes eligible to officially compete for the U.S. in international races and national team qualifying events.
Best of all, they were also able to celebrate their success with Amir, who was cared for during the race by Elizabeth’s sister, Kaitlyn, who lives in Houston.
“It was a special day,” Zouhair said. “It was the first time I was listed as a U.S. runner with the American flag next to my name. It was something I had always dreamed of when I thought about coming to America. And to have Elizabeth run so well, too, really made it a special day for both of us.”
A Long and Winding Journey
Zouhair discovered his talent as a teen growing up in Tighassaline, Khenifra, Morocco, and emerged as one of the top high school runners in the country, eventually placing 14th in the U-20 race at the World Cross Country Championships in Bydgoszcz, Poland, as a 17-year-old in 2013. He continued on an upward trajectory as a college student, running 13:51 in the 5,000 meters as a 19-year-old and earning the silver medal in the event at the World University Games in Seoul, South Korea.
Despite his success, Zouhair says training and racing always seemed to be a constant struggle because of a lack of guidance and marginal support. He dreamed of running in the U.S. collegiate system, but it wasn’t until 2019, at the age of 23, that he enrolled at Florida State University.

She’s been on two Olympic teams and won the Boston Marathon, but Des Linden is still a rookie when it comes to ultra events.
In her first 100-miler, the Javelina Jundred on October 31 (stretching into November 1 for some runners) in Fountain Hills, Arizona, Linden finished as the ninth woman in 16 hours and 58 minutes.
Linden ran strongly for the first three laps of the five-lap race. She took over the lead at about the 40-mile mark and held onto that lead for the next 20 miles.
She hit 60.3 miles at 8:01:12, an average of 7:58 per mile pace for more than twice the marathon distance over the hilly trails.
But at the aid station at 60.3 miles, Linden sat down while her crew tended to her. She changed shoes and took about five minutes to get up and start running again. Within a half a mile of leaving the aid station, she was walking, and two female runners, Katie Asmuth and Carla Molinaro, passed her.
The final 40 miles took her 8 hours and 57 minutes.
Although the daylight hours were primarily dry on the desert loop, heavy rain drenched the course at the start and after night fell, drawing comparisons to the 2018 Boston Marathon, which Linden won, in a nor’easter.
The women’s race was incredibly close.
Heather Jackson, 42, won in 13:48:29, averaging 8:17 pace. Molinaro was second in 13:49:24, after Jackson overtook her in the final quarter mile of the race. Both earned “golden tickets” for the Western States Endurance Run, the famed 100-miler in June that goes from Olympic Valley to Auburn, California.
The men’s race was also close: Rob Molke, 35, finished in 12:11:30, holding off Noah Dusseau, who was runner-up in 12:12:57. They also earned “golden tickets” for Western States.
Linden will likely be motivated to solve the puzzle of the 100-mile distance, as she was early in her marathon career when she wanted to master 26.2 miles.
Her training wasn’t ideal leading up to Javelina, although she had several two-day stretches when she ran 30 miles one day and 20 the next.
She was aware she would need to adjust her goals if she started to struggle in the later miles.
“Just get to the finish. I think that’s super important,” she said in a phone interview with Runner’s World on October 29. “I think if I can run the whole time, that’s going to be great. And then if it’s going really well, I would love to get a golden ticket. But those are just as flexible as the plan. I know that even finishing can be something that all of a sudden comes into question. It’s just so different from anything I've done.”
Linden was also looking forward to the relaxed vibe and the chance to be around her crew and other runners.
“As a runner, you make these friends and they become your community,” she said. “But everyone lives [all over] the country. It’s hard to meet up with people, and so this is really just an excuse to hang out with a bunch of people who are really fun. It’ll be good. A good hang, no matter what.”

Ask any marathoner: There is nothing like the energy of race weekend to get you amped up to keep on running. Feeling the weight of that finisher’s medal hanging around your neck has a magical way of erasing all the aches and exhaustion you pushed through for the past few hours (not to mention the past several months of training).
But what you do in the hours and days immediately following 26.2 miles can determine how quickly you bounce back—not only physically but also how soon you’ll feel emotionally ready to get moving again. Marathons are draining, and that finish-line euphoria won’t keep sustaining you through continuous daily runs if you don’t let yourself recover fully.
After conquering 14 marathon finish lines in all seasons and a few back-to-back marathons too, I’ve learned a few key lessons about how to successfully get back to running postrace. Keep these in mind if you’ve just crossed a marathon off your list and want to lace up your running shoes again soon.
Don’t: Kick your feet up the entire rest of race day.
The first time I ran the New York City Marathon, I lived in a fifth-floor walk-up apartment on the Upper East Side. Going down those stairs the next day was excruciating, but I went outside anyway and went for a walk—and my legs felt immensely better a day later, compared with when I didn’t take those steps after other races.
Obviously, you should give yourself some downtime and relax after a marathon, but when I make a point to walk around more often right after a race and to do some other light activity (like easy pedaling on my Peloton) over the following few days, it always helps my legs feel way better sooner. Sitting on the couch all day will only increase your stiffness.
Do: Treat yourself!
Regardless of whether you hit a PR, qualified for Boston, or barely made it over the finish line, completing a marathon is a big accomplishment. I’ve found that taking some time after 26.2 to celebrate and appreciate my body for what it can do—and my mind for what it can push through—is an important step before jumping right back into running. When I push ahead without taking joy and pride in what I achieved, I wind up feeling run down and unmotivated.
If you feel like having a decadent meal and celebratory beers as part of that acknowledgment, Jeff Gaudette, owner and head coach at RunnersConnect, says go for it! But to feel up to running again soon, have something nutritious first.
“The focus on recovery needs to be more dialed in if you're going to do another race soon,” he says. “That means nutrition and refueling a little more diligently. You can still enjoy pizza and beer, but make sure you get some protein and healthy carbs beforehand.”
Research backs this nutrient combo up: One 2018 study in Nutrients found that eating both carbs and protein immediately postrace helped marathoners’ physical fatigue, mental energy, and soreness improve within three days compared with those who ate carbs alone.
Don’t: Skimp on R&R.
Your body just did a lot; give it some extra TLC to help your muscles recover faster. Gaudette recommends trying out all the “little recovery tricks”—ice baths, dips in a hot tub, a massage—and seeing what helps you get back to 100 percent faster.

ExxonMobil (XOM +2.16%) just raised its quarterly dividend by another 3.9%, extending its growth streak to an industry-leading 44 consecutive years. That's a longer streak than 95% of companies in the S&P 500.
However, it was a very modest raise compared to its free cash flow, which has surged 90% year-over-year to $39 billion over the last nine months. That gap between the modest dividend increase and surging free cash flow isn't an accident, and what it says about how Exxon runs its cash is worth a closer look.
Image source: Getty Images.
Focused on the long term
ExxonMobil generated $19.1 billion in free cash flow during the third quarter alone, nearly as much as it produced during the first nine months of last year ($20.6 billion). That's enough cash to cover a year's worth of dividends with room to spare ($17.2 billion annually at its current $4.3 billion quarterly run rate). Clearly, Exxon has the capacity to deliver a much higher dividend increase.
However, the company's dividend payment is a fixed expense. Its cash flow, on the other hand, is highly variable. It has surged this year due to higher oil prices and refining margins caused by supply disruptions in the Middle East. When those disruptions finally ease, pricing and margins will fall, as will Exxon's free cash flow.

Yeman Crippa of Italy, who was the last to hang with Almgren, placed second in 2:06:14 (and then promptly vomited). Kamohelo Mofolo of Lesotho outkicked defending champion Benson Kipruto in the final meters to finish third in a personal best of 2:06:26, one second ahead of Kipruto.

Conner Mantz, running his first marathon since setting the U.S. record last year in Chicago, was 11th in 2:07:27.

Six weeks ago, he won the world half marathon championship in a national record of 58:06. He even boasts an 800-meter best of 1:45, a borderline world-class time that none of his competitors has run.
Despite that pedigree, none of the seasoned marathoners made a serious effort to drop Almgren far out from the finish. Fifteen men remained bunched at the 35K (21.7 miles) mark.
The real racing didn’t start until defending champ Kipruto surged to a 4:38 24th mile. That led to him, Almgren, and Crippa separating. Almgren, who trains by kilometers instead of miles, waited until just before 40K (24.9 miles) to take the lead for the first time. Crippa was able to stick with him for another kilometer, but right as Crippa snuck a look back on Central Park South, Almgren surged again and ran unchallenged to the finish.
When asked after the race whether he thought the moderate first 30 kilometers was playing into his hands, Almgren said, “Kinda, but not really. I mean, this is my first marathon. I don’t really know how it’s supposed to feel at those different points.”
At 20 miles, Almgren said, “I was like, ‘Shit, I’m tired. Why are my legs feeling like this?’” But a few minutes later, “I just started feeling like, ‘It’s pretty easy to respond now to the moves.’ So somewhere around there I felt like, ‘Okay, this might be my day.’”

Ciara Mageean, an Irish runner who set national records in the 800 meters, mile, and 1500 meters, died November 1, according to a social media post from her family. She was 34.
Mageean was diagnosed with stage 4 bowel cancer in May 2025.
She competed in two Olympics, in 2016 and 2021, in the 1500 meters, but she could not race at the Games in 2024, due to an Achilles injury.
The timing of that injury was unfortunate, because from 2023 to early 2024, Mageean was at the height of her powers.

In May of 2024, she ran 1:58.51 for 800 meters and the next month, she won the European Championships 1500 meters. Her final professional race was a Diamond League 2,000 meters in July 2024 in Monaco.
Mageean announced her cancer in a July 2025 post on Instagram, in which only her right arm, hooked up to a tube, was visible. The Olympic rings were tattooed on the inside of her wrist.
In June, Mageean released a book, My Greatest Race, about her cancer diagnosis. It became an all-Ireland bestseller.
Mageean was sponsored by New Balance, and at times, New Balance Boston athletes would cross paths with Mageean during altitude training stints in Flagstaff, Arizona. American miler Elle St. Pierre said she admired how tenacious Mageean was, training hard even when she couldn’t run due to injury.
“She was just very resilient,” St. Pierre said. “Through a number of injuries, she always came back so fast, and I feel like she she handled that mentally really well, too, and she’d still be training. That’s a really tough part of the sport, but something that really that stood out to me.”

Mark Coogan, coach of New Balance Boston, remembers enjoying a Guinness after the New Balance Indoor Games and laughing with Mageean.
“I saw her more as as a friend and someone to root for than someone that we were trying to beat all the time,” Coogan said.
Mageean set her mile national record in the race where Faith Kipyegon of Kenya set the world record.

Exxon Is Up 59% This Year After Another Beat. This Is How High It Can Go.
Exxon just crushed earnings again and hit a new 52-week high, yet analysts are divided on whether the historic rally still has room to run or has already priced in every piece of good news.
Exxon Mobil (NYSE:XOM | XOM Price Prediction) beat earnings estimates again this morning. Shares rose to $188.30 in early trading, which puts the year-to-date gain at 59.59%.
The 24/7 Wall St. price target for Exxon is $173.08. That means -5.57% downside from the $183.29 close our model used.
We have high confidence in this rating. The beat moved our target up sharply. One week ago, the model sat at $140.77 with a sell rating. Higher earnings and record-level cash flow closed most of the gap between Exxon’s fundamentals and its share price.
Why We Could Be Wrong
Our 24/7 Wall St. price target is below where Exxon trades today. Upside could come from Guyana and Permian volume growth or from oil prices that stay higher for longer. Treat our target as one datapoint among many. The bull case below explains why Exxon could beat our model.
Refining Boom Drives a Clean Third-Quarter Beat
Over the past week the stock added 5.65%. It is up 16.7% over the past month and 66.34% over the past year. Today’s move drove it above its prior 52-week high of $184.88, far from the $109.34 low.
Adjusted EPS of $4.23 exceeded the $3.98 consensus. Revenue of $110.50B beat the $104.03B estimate, and free cash flow reached $19.10B. Reuters credited a war-driven refining surge for the results. WTI averaged $97.31 in September, compared with $60.04 in January.
Why Bulls See $213 Ahead
Exxon’s growth engine is real. Permian output hit a record above 1.8 Moebd, and the company plans 9% CAGR through 2030. A fifth Guyana FPSO added 250 Kbd of capacity. Golden Pass LNG volumes are rising, and Exxon has announced a $20B buyback for 2027.
CEO Darren Woods called the gains “lasting improvements, not simply the result of favorable prices and margins.” Among analysts, 3 rate the stock a higher buy and 7 rate it a buy. Our one-year bull case is $185.20, and our five-year bull path reaches $213.20.
Risks That Could Pull Exxon Back to $150
Most analysts sit on the sidelines, with 15 hold ratings and a consensus target of $179.41. Middle East disruptions have cost $921M so far this year. Impairments total $1.08B, and chemical margins remain under pressure. The EIA expects oil prices to reflect a larger risk premium while Hormuz flows recover, but that premium could fade.
GAAP EPS of $3.72 trailed adjusted EPS. Bulls would note that the $2.54B of negative timing effects came from unsettled derivatives, and those effects tend to reverse. The bear case is $150.68.
How Exxon Compares to Chevron and ConocoPhillips
Chevron (NYSE:CVX) is Exxon’s closest integrated rival. It posted adjusted EPS of $5.28 against a $4.826 estimate, and it trades at a richer multiple with a higher yield.
ConocoPhillips (NYSE:COP) is the pure upstream contrast. It trades at a slightly lower multiple even though it lacks Exxon’s refining buffer. Against this group, our 24/7 Wall St. price target looks reasonable.
Why Our Rating Stays at Hold After a Historic Run
The 24/7 Wall St. price target of $173.08 has a hold rating with 90% confidence. What drives the call is that consensus expects slightly lower forward earnings even after a 59.59% year-to-date rally.
The stock would look more attractive if Guyana and Permian growth raises 2027 estimates.

"The housing market is haunted," according to David Kelly, the chief global strategist at J.P. Morgan Asset Management.
He lists the ghosts in his widely read Oct. 26 research note: more than a decade of too-easy money, tariffs, and immigration policies that raise the cost of building homes while limiting the number of people who need them, and a Fed whose rate swings hit housing harder than almost anything else.
The one that should get the most attention is the people who aren't showing up. Kelly said he expects U.S. population growth of just 800,000 a year over the next few years. With an average household of about 2.5 people, he writes, that "implies a demographic need for just 320,000 new housing units per year," compared with roughly 1 million per year in the first two decades of this century.
That cuts against the story most Americans have heard about housing: that the country simply hasn't built enough. Zillow estimated in July the U.S. was about 4.7 million homes short as of 2024, based on how many families are doubled up with unrelated people compared with how many homes sit vacant for rent or sale. Kelly's read is that the country is "still in a situation of net excess supply."
Thursday's GDP report bore that out, Kelly told Fortune by email. Homebuilding fell again in the third quarter, "marking the 8th decline in residential construction in the last 10 quarters." But "the homebuilding decline is still relatively modest compared to the very fast increase in AI-related capital spending," he said.
Where the people went
In the first 20 years of this century, Kelly wrote, the U.S. population grew by an average of 2.4 million people a year—about 1.5 million from births minus deaths and about 900,000 from net immigration. The natural increase peaked at 520,000 in 2025, he writes, and has likely resumed a steady decline as the population ages and birth rates fall.
Immigration swung harder. Net international migration fell to 1.3 million in the year through July 2025 from 2.7 million a year earlier, and the Census Bureau projected it would be about 321,000 by July 2026 if trends continued. Kelly estimated that deportations are now almost canceling out legal net immigration, which is still positive but smaller. He said he expects that to hold "regardless of the outcome of the midterm elections," because enforcement is largely up to the administration, and Congress and the White House are unlikely to agree on an immigration reform bill.
The empty-house signs
Kelly pointed to vacancies. Over the past four years, he writes, the rental vacancy rate rose from 5.6% to 7.3%, and the homeowner vacancy rate from 0.8% to 1.2%. Census figures released Wednesday put rental vacancy at 7.6% in the third quarter, up from 7.1% a year earlier. Between the second quarter of 2024 and the second quarter of 2026, he writes, the housing stock grew by about 2.8 million units.
Buyers have thinned out. You’d think so.
In 2024, voters approved Amendment 3, enshrining abortion rights in the state constitution. Republican lawmakers responded by putting another amendment on the ballot.
So we’re doing this again?
Yes, but not quite the same way.
Amendment 3 would repeal those protections and restore a ban on most abortions, with limited exceptions. It would also constitutionally prohibit gender-affirming medical care for minors.
Wait, it’s also Amendment 3?

This time around, a yes vote bans abortion and a no vote keeps it legal.

An August SLU/YouGov poll found 43% in favor, 44% opposed and 13% undecided.

A bridge stretches across the Missouri River at Chamberlain, South Dakota, on Sept. 29 (Makenzie Huber/South Dakota Searchlight).
Downstream Missouri River states have worried for decades about receiving an insufficient flow of water from upstream dams.
Now they’re worried their share of water could be further diminished by potential pipelines for dry Western states.
The concern is the basis of a dispute about the U.S. House version of the federal Water Resources Development Act. A provision in the bill would require approval from all governors in Missouri River states to study or construct a project that moves water from the river or its tributaries to a non-Missouri River state.
The bill has passed the House and awaits action in the Senate, where a Senate version of the legislation lacks the controversial provision.
Missouri lawmaker and group support provision
The House bill’s definition of “Missouri River states” includes not only the seven states where the river flows — Montana, North Dakota, South Dakota, Nebraska, Iowa, Kansas and Missouri — but also Colorado, Minnesota and Wyoming, which have land within the river’s 530,000-square-mile drainage basin.
A downstream lawmaker, U.S. Rep. Sam Graves, R-Missouri, sponsors the House bill. Supporters of the controversial provision include an organization in his state, the Coalition to Protect the Missouri River.
Shane Kinne is the coalition’s executive director. He said Missourians’ concerns about water shortages are not hypothetical. For the last four years, the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers has limited water releases from upper Missouri River reservoirs, affecting commercial barge traffic downstream.
Kinne said Missouri River Basin states should collaborate “so we can manage the resource together and protect ourselves from Western states looking for water.”
“If this isn’t the proposal, let’s bring some ideas to address this concern,” he said.
Joint opposition: Dakotas, Montana, Wyoming, Colorado, Utah
Kinne’s view faces opposition in upstream states.
The governors of Montana, North Dakota and South Dakota — where the Missouri River flows through a series of dams and reservoirs — recently joined with governors in the Missouri River Basin states of Colorado and Wyoming on a letter opposing the House provision.
Also signing the letter was the governor of Utah, which is not part of the Missouri River Basin. Supermarkets in Belgium and Sweden reported sudden changes in the temperatures of their fridges and freezers on Monday, sparking fears of a cyberattack similar to those that recently occurred in France.
Delhaize, which is owned by Dutch retailer Ahold Delhaize, confirmed that an “IT incident” took place at about 40 of its stores in Belgium on Sunday night, impacting the refrigeration systems, Belgian newswire Belga reported. A small number of Carrefour Belgium and Spar supermarkets also reported a similar issue, Belga said.

Unlike garden-variety hackers targeting individual investors, TraderTraitor uses a strategy known as Big Game Hunting, cybersecurity experts say, helped by AI to seek out high-value crypto businesses to compromise. They’ve been so remarkably successful that the revenues they generate could be funding nearly half of North Korea’s banned weapons programs.
“This particular group looks for a big haul,” said Park Seong-su, Staff Threat Researcher at Zscaler, a cybersecurity firm. “They target crypto-related businesses, gain an understanding of their infrastructure and then tamper with it — or fund transfer processes — to execute a large-scale theft.”
With new AI tools “the barriers to such skills have dropped significantly, while the speed at which these operations can be carried out has increased tremendously,” Park added.
For decades, North Korea has picked its best and brightest students to join its hacking teams, training them at specialized institutions like Moranbong College in Pyongyang, defectors and experts say, to create an army which is now believed to be responsible for 89% of reported crypto hack losses this year, according to Chainalysis.
From running laptop farms in the US to stealing billions of crypto in less than 30 minutes, its hackers have become one of the most important sources of revenue for North Korea, which is isolated from the global financial system due to rafts of sanctions over Kim’s nuclear weapons and ballistic missile programs.
North Korea’s other income sources, such as trade with China and even the military relationship with Russia, are now dwarfed in significance by crypto cash. Once, Pyongyang was smuggling cigarettes and forging US dollar bills to stay afloat — now its hackers bring in billions in pure profit from a single successful heist.
